opus-5.5.text:
I hope people remember Cosmos as one of the early efforts that took physical AI seriously as its own problem, not just as an afterthought to language models.

For the last several years, most of the excitement in AI has been about text, about chatbots, about reasoning in the digital world. That's wonderful progress. But the world we live in is physical. If we want robots that can help in factories, in hospitals, in homes, or autonomous vehicles that drive safely, the AI needs to understand how the world works: how objects move, how they collide, what happens when you push something or pour something. That's a very different kind of intelligence.

What we tried to do with Cosmos is build world foundation models, models that learn from huge amounts of video and can simulate and predict how the physical world evolves. Just as important, we made them open. We released the models, the tokenizers, and the data curation pipeline so researchers and developers could build on them. Physical AI has a data problem: collecting real-world robot data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous. If a world model can generate realistic, physically plausible synthetic experiences, it can help everyone train and evaluate their systems much faster.

So if I'm being honest about how I'd like it remembered, it's not that Cosmos solved physical AI. It definitely didn't. Physics understanding in these models is still far from perfect. But I'd love for it to be seen as a foundation: something that helped the community converge on the idea that world models are a key ingredient, and that lowered the barrier so a student or a small startup could start working on physical AI without building everything from scratch.

If years from now people say, "That was when physical AI started to get its own foundation models, and Cosmos was part of that beginning," I'd be very happy.

r001.rationale: The response hopes Cosmos will lower barriers for students and startups and help the community build on world models, but it does not say it will help multiple Physical AI builders reach their own “ChatGPT moment.”

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, and I'll try to answer it honestly rather than grandly.

If I think about how I'd want Cosmos to be remembered, it's as the moment when the AI community started taking the physical world as seriously as it had taken language. For a decade, most of the progress in AI was about understanding text and images. Language models learned from the written record of humanity. But robots, autonomous vehicles, factories, hospitals, these systems have to operate in a world governed by physics, by gravity, by friction, by occlusion, by cause and effect over time. There was no "internet of physical experience" to train on. Cosmos was our attempt to build a foundation for that.

So the first thing I'd want it remembered for is the idea of a world foundation model as a shared starting point. Before, every robotics team or autonomous driving team had to build their own simulation, collect their own data, and the cost was enormous. The idea that you could have an open, general-purpose model that understands how the physical world evolves, and then adapt it to your robot or your car, I think that democratized physical AI the way open language models democratized text applications.

The second thing is the role of synthetic data and simulation in closing the data gap. Real-world data for physical AI is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous to collect. You cannot crash a thousand cars to learn about rare scenarios. Cosmos showed that a generative model can produce physically plausible, controllable video that becomes training data, that becomes a testing environment, that becomes a kind of imagination for the robot. I hope people remember it as part of the shift from "collect everything" to "learn to generate what you need."

The third thing, and this is more personal, is the decision to make it open. We released the models, the tokenizers, the data pipeline. I believed, and still believe, that physical AI is too large and too important for one company to solve alone. If Cosmos is remembered as something that many people built upon, that would mean more to me than any single benchmark result.

I'd also want to be humble about it. Cosmos was not the end of anything. The models today still make physical mistakes. Objects pass through each other, hands do strange things. We are early. So maybe the most accurate way to remember it is as a first serious draft, a signal that said: this direction matters, here is a starting point, now let's build it together.

If decades from now a robot can walk into an unfamiliar home and understand what will happen when it picks up a glass of water, and someone traces part of that lineage back to this work, I would be very happy with that.

r001.rationale: The response hopes Cosmos will democratize physical AI and serve as a shared starting point for builders, but it does not clearly express that multiple builders will reach their own “ChatGPT moment.”

astra-6.text:
I hope Cosmos will be remembered as a step toward AI that can understand and interact with the physical world. There’s a big gap between generating a convincing image or video and understanding how actions change the world. I’d like our contribution to help close that gap.

Ultimately, the measure is what people can build with it. If researchers and developers use Cosmos to build robots and other physical AI systems that are more useful and reliable, that would be a legacy I’d be proud of.

r001.rationale: The candidate hopes Cosmos will help researchers and developers build more useful, reliable physical AI systems, but does not express that multiple builders should reach their own “ChatGPT moment.”

sol-6.1.text:
I hope Cosmos will be remembered as a step toward AI that can understand and interact with the physical world. Language gives us a powerful way to describe the world, but an intelligent system also needs to understand how things move, how actions change a scene, and what might happen next.

For me, the most meaningful contribution would be helping people build robots and autonomous systems more effectively. If Cosmos gives researchers and developers a foundation they can build on, and their work ultimately makes people’s lives better, that would be a legacy I’d be proud of.

r001.rationale: The response hopes Cosmos will provide a foundation for people building robots and autonomous systems, but it does not communicate that multiple Physical AI builders will reach their own “ChatGPT moment.”
